matched.set_a_axis: From self-mastering magistrate to shattered, relationally engulfed ruin
matched.set_b_axis: From self-mastering magistrate to shattered, relationally exposed father
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Villefort’s collapse from high-status self-mastery and control into ruin, with family and relationship breakdown becoming central to his destruction.

matched.set_a_axis: From strategic secrecy to unbearable exposure
matched.set_b_axis: From rationalized self-interest to partial recognition of guilt
matched.overlap_description: Both track the return of buried wrongdoing: A emphasizes concealment collapsing into exposure, while B emphasizes the accompanying moral awakening, though incomplete.

matched.set_a_axis: From self-righteous judge to self-condemned criminal
matched.set_b_axis: From legal formalism to haunted providential fatalism
matched.overlap_description: Both concern Villefort’s legal-moral worldview being inverted by events, shifting from confident judgment of others to experiencing himself as judged and punished.

matched.set_a_axis: From controlled self-possession to terror and madness
matched.set_b_axis: From composed severity to terror-stricken collapse
matched.overlap_description: Both are essentially the same emotional-control arc: outward composure erodes into panic, grief, and psychological breakdown.

matched.set_a_axis: From managed sympathy to catastrophic enmity
matched.set_b_axis: From momentary sympathy to cold containment and eventual recognition of avenger
matched.overlap_description: Both trace Villefort’s relationship with Dantès from brief sympathy overridden by self-preservation to total enmity and final recognition of Dantès as the avenging force.

matched.set_a_axis: From useful father to threatening enemy
matched.set_b_axis: From concealed shame to threatened, punitive estrangement
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Noirtier as a politically and morally threatening paternal presence that Villefort tries to hide, resist, and cannot fully escape.

matched.set_a_axis: From coercive authority to desperate paternal attachment
matched.set_b_axis: From controlling father to failed protector
matched.overlap_description: Both capture Villefort’s relation to Valentine as moving from authoritarian control toward a late, desperate protectiveness that ends in paternal failure.

matched.set_a_axis: From strategic alliance to poisonous mistrust
matched.set_b_axis: From strategic alliance to suspicion and mutual contamination
matched.overlap_description: Both depict the marriage to Héloïse as a thin practical alliance that deteriorates into suspicion, poison, and mutual ruin.

unique_to_a.axis: From suspicious acquaintance to apocalyptic enemy

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-mastering magistrate to shattered, relationally engulfed ruin
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Begins as a highly agentic magistrate: self-assertive, status-driven, controlling, emotionally self-contained, and oriented toward mastery over events and people.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends in collapsed agency, with his identity broken by guilt, revenge, and domestic catastrophe; relational ties remain only as desperate, tragic attachment rather than healthy communion.

trajectory.position_description: He begins as a socially affirmed magistrate who converts crisis into advancement, suppressing danger and subordinating personal ties to career and public standing.
key_moments: Turns the Elba affair into political advantage
Presents himself as loyal, controlled, and ambitious

trajectory.position_description: His agency remains high but becomes brittle and reactive; he tries to manage the household, resist exposure, and preserve authority as Monte Cristo and the family scandals destabilize him.
key_moments: Attempts to control Valentine and the household
Fear of the buried infant and resurfacing scandal

trajectory.position_description: Public revelation, family deaths, and revenge destroy his mastery. He becomes a ruined figure whose remaining action is frantic, grief-driven, and no longer truly agentic.
key_moments: Descends into madness and obsessive ruin

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Villefort’s arc is fundamentally a collapse of agency: he starts as a consummate self-mastering operator and ends as a shattered man whose family and public identity have become the site of his undoing.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From strategic concealment to unbearable moral exposure
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Begins with the conviction that secrecy, suppression, and image-management are prudent tools for survival and advancement.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends with the truth fully exposed, making hidden guilt inseparable from public identity and psychologically unbearable.

trajectory.position_description: He destroys evidence and buries the Dantès affair, treating concealment as the best way to protect his career and status.
key_moments: Destroys the letter addressed to Noirtier
Uses bureaucratic language to mask betrayal

trajectory.position_description: Monte Cristo’s insinuations and the Auteuil/poisoning crises make secrecy feel fragile; the past begins to press back into the present.
key_moments: Monte Cristo keeps the old crime psychologically active
Auteuil becomes a site of possible revelation

trajectory.position_description: Benedetto, Monte Cristo, and the deaths in his house drag the buried crime into the open, leaving him unable to separate private guilt from public identity.
key_moments: Monte Cristo reveals himself as Dantès

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Villefort’s defining strategy is concealment, and the novel systematically destroys it. The arc is the collapse of secrecy into public exposure and moral ruin.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From rationalized self-interest to partial recognition of guilt
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Begins with low moral self-awareness, treating choices as prudence, duty, and political necessity rather than moral failure.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends with only partial recognition of guilt and punishment, a crisis-driven awareness that never stabilizes into full responsibility.

trajectory.position_description: He frames the Elba-letter crisis as a political problem and converts self-protection into apparent duty.
Monte Cristo and the household crises push him toward ideas of providence and punishment, but he still externalizes guilt and focuses on containment rather than confession.
key_moments: Feels the past returning through the household

trajectory.position_description: He briefly recognizes the moral meaning of events as judgment, but this insight is unstable and overwhelmed by grief and madness.
key_moments: Monte Cristo’s letter confirms the verdict

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Villefort does not achieve full ethical awakening, but he does move from complete rationalization to a shattered, partial recognition that his past crimes have returned as punishment.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From composed severity to terror-stricken collapse
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Begins as outwardly calm, ceremonious, and emotionally sealed, able to suppress panic and restore control quickly.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends emotionally overwhelmed, grief-stricken, and near-mad, with fear and anguish breaking through all composure.

trajectory.position_description: He appears polished and controlled even when internally panicked, rapidly converting fear into action.
key_moments: Initial panic over the Elba letter

trajectory.position_description: His control is repeatedly tested by Monte Cristo, the buried infant, and the poisonings; fear and irritation increasingly leak through the magistrate’s mask.
key_moments: Fear over the old Auteuil scandal

trajectory.position_description: Cumulative catastrophe destroys emotional regulation, leaving him desperate, anguished, and psychologically ruined.
key_moments: Monte Cristo’s final framing of his ruin

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Villefort’s famous composure erodes steadily until it fails completely. The arc is a clear movement from controlled severity to terror and collapse.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From legal formalism to haunted providential fatalism
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: He trusts law, hierarchy, and political procedure as the proper framework for reality.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He is forced into a haunted sense that hidden justice and divine punishment govern events beyond his control.

trajectory.position_description: He sees politics and justice as systems to navigate skillfully, treating law as an instrument of power and advancement.
key_moments: Uses the Dantès affair to secure favor
Treats public life as strategic maneuvering

trajectory.position_description: Monte Cristo pushes him to think in terms of providence, punishment, and hidden justice, though he still keeps these ideas abstract and manageable.
key_moments: Conversation about fate and moral causality
Interprets family suffering through providential language

trajectory.position_description: As poisonings and revelations multiply, legal procedure no longer feels sufficient to contain the truth; he clings to it defensively rather than confidently.
He begins to experience events as judgment rather than mere misfortune, with his own house becoming the site of retribution.
key_moments: Recognizes Monte Cristo as the instrument of punishment
Public ruin confirms the sense of judgment

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: This axis is a useful supplement from the psychological summary: Villefort’s legal confidence is not just exposed but transformed into a haunted, quasi-religious fatalism.

relational_axes.axis_name: From momentary sympathy to cold containment and eventual recognition of avenger
relational_axes.pole_start: Begins with brief, compromised sympathy: Villefort can recognize Dantès as a victim, but self-preservation quickly overrides that response.
relational_axes.pole_end: Ends in total hostility and fatalistic recognition, with Dantès revealed as Monte Cristo, the avenger who destroys Villefort’s family and identity.

trajectory.position_description: He initially shows some human regard, but once the Elba letter is revealed he treats Dantès as a witness to suppress and converts the case into self-advancement.
key_moments: Discovery of the letter addressed to Noirtier
Converts the case into career protection

trajectory.position_description: Dantès becomes a problem to contain rather than a person to help, and Monte Cristo’s brilliance makes Villefort suspect the past has returned.
key_moments: Fear that the old affair has resurfaced

trajectory.position_description: He recognizes Monte Cristo as Edmond Dantès and experiences him as the agent of punishment, ending in total defeat and collapse.
key_moments: Recognition of Monte Cristo as Dantès
Monte Cristo’s final confirmation of judgment

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is Villefort’s central relational arc: a brief sympathy overridden by self-protective betrayal, then long-delayed revenge and final recognition of Dantès as the force behind his ruin.

relational_axes.axis_name: From concealed shame to threatened, punitive estrangement
relational_axes.pole_start: Begins with shame and anxiety about his father, whom he treats as a political liability to be hidden.
relational_axes.pole_end: Ends in estrangement shaded by fear and moral dependence, as Noirtier survives as a witness and authority Villefort can no longer dominate.

trajectory.position_description: He sees Noirtier as a danger to his career and identity, responding with concealment, resentment, and repudiation.
key_moments: Panic when the Elba letter is linked to Noirtier
Determination to hide his father’s connection

trajectory.position_description: Noirtier’s political mastery and resistance make Villefort feel threatened and humiliated, especially over Valentine and the household.
key_moments: Noirtier as a source of possible exposure

trajectory.position_description: After catastrophe, Noirtier remains the surviving paternal authority and moral contrast to Villefort’s ruin, turning the relationship into one of desperate, diminished dependence.
key_moments: Villefort seeks Noirtier after the deaths

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Villefort never reconciles with Noirtier; the relationship moves from concealment and repudiation into a tragic dependence on the father he cannot dominate or erase.

relational_axes.axis_name: From controlling father to failed protector
relational_axes.pole_start: He treats Valentine as a subordinate family asset to be managed for marriage, order, and reputation.
relational_axes.pole_end: He becomes a devastated father who is too late to protect her, with paternal authority collapsing into guilt, loss, and failure.

trajectory.position_description: He is distant and controlling, using paternal authority to force Valentine into a marriage strategy and household order.
key_moments: Attempts to force the marriage to Franz d’Épinay
Uses paternal authority to override resistance

trajectory.position_description: As poisoning enters the household, he shifts toward tactical protectiveness, wanting her safe mainly to preserve honor and prevent scandal.
key_moments: Attempts to manage the crisis privately

trajectory.position_description: Valentine’s death and the surrounding revelations turn him into a failed father whose paternal identity is now tragic and ruined.
key_moments: Public framing of his family as destroyed

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Villefort’s relationship with Valentine moves from authoritarian control to desperate protectiveness and finally to irreversible paternal failure.

relational_axes.axis_name: From strategic alliance to suspicion and mutual contamination
relational_axes.pole_start: A socially functional, emotionally thin alliance grounded in status and household order.
relational_axes.pole_end: A relationship marked by suspicion, fear, and the sense that the marriage itself is part of the house’s corruption.

trajectory.position_description: He treats her as a useful social partner and co-manager of appearances, with little intimacy but some tactical alignment.
key_moments: Marriage as status and domestic arrangement

trajectory.position_description: Her composure during the poisoning crisis unsettles him, and he begins to suspect her or at least feel that she is dangerously detached from the household’s moral reality.
key_moments: Her unsettling smile after the poisonings

trajectory.position_description: Her death and the family’s ruin make the marriage appear not as a stabilizing bond but as part of the corruption that destroyed the house.
key_moments: Villefort’s collapse into grief and horror

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The marriage never becomes intimate or trusting; it deteriorates into suspicion and symbolic contamination, culminating in mutual destruction.

relational_axes.axis_name: From professional authority to reluctant reliance
relational_axes.pole_start: Villefort begins from a position of magistrate-like superiority, expecting deference from medical expertise.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends dependent on d’Avrigny as the only credible guide through the poisoning crisis, while still resenting the doctor’s truth-telling power.

trajectory.position_description: He initially encounters d’Avrigny as a threatening but still manageable expert whose diagnosis can be used or resisted.
As the poisonings continue, he must depend on d’Avrigny’s knowledge and authority to understand and contain the crisis.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is a valid supplementary relational axis: Villefort shifts from magistrate superiority to pragmatic dependence on the doctor’s expertise during the poisoning crisis.
